Underwater electromagnetic signatures arise from induced and permanent magnetizations, eddy currents, corrosion-related currents, and electrical machinery onboard.
The Earth's magnetic field induces magnetizations in ferromagnetic ship hulls, contributing significantly to magnetic signatures.
Finite element (FE) methods are the preferred numerical technique for detailed modeling of ferromagnetic, eddy-current, and stray magnetic fields.
FE models require high mesh densities and numerical accuracy to predict fields near 1 Tesla amplitude at onboard sources and picotesla levels at threat sensor locations.
Permanent magnetization modeling in FE is challenging; two techniques include scaling induced magnetization or using large anhysteretic permeability constants.
Physical scale models have been used since World War II and provide more accurate signature predictions than FE models.
Thickness scaling and permeability-thickness modeling are two methods to construct magnetic scale models.
Verification involves peer review, comparison with analytic solutions, and cross-model comparisons; validation requires comparison with full-scale measurements.
Scale models typically predict signatures within 10% of full-scale ship measurements, considered reliable for design.
Degaussing coils actively cancel magnetic signatures; the M-coil effect quantifies signature change per ampere of coil current.
Signature reduction design must balance cost, weight, reliability, maintainability, and performance constraints.
The design process includes preliminary design with analytic models, detailed design with numerical models, final design, validation, and realization.
Design validation using full-scale prototypes has been reduced due to budget constraints, increasing risk of undetected design flaws.
Over- or under-design of signature reduction systems can lead to excessive costs or vulnerability to detection and mines.
Lessons from engineering failures emphasize the importance of critical thinking and not relying solely on computational models.
